one_liner: 2018 course-project AVX-512/AVX2 bitonic merge sort for power-of-two numeric arrays; 7.7x std::sort on 1M 32-bit ints in its own report.
what_it_does: Sorts arrays of int32, int64, float and double, and key-value pairs of those types, with hand-written AVX-512 (namespace avx512) or AVX2 (namespace avx2, not avx256 as the README says) intrinsics; it also offers a single-column ORDER BY that sorts (key, row index) pairs and then gathers records. The API is not iterator based: SIMDSort(size_t N, T*& arr) takes a reference to a pointer to a 64-byte-aligned buffer whose length is a power of two, and it may repoint that pointer at a different buffer when it returns.
how_it_is_fast: Phase 1 loads 16 ZMM registers (a 256-element block of 32-bit keys, or 8 registers of 64-bit keys), runs a branch-free bitonic sorting network across registers with vector min/max, then an in-register 16x16 transpose leaves sorted runs of 16 (8 for 64-bit). Phase 2 runs log2(N/16) out-of-place merge passes, each merging two runs a register at a time with an in-register bitonic merge network into a ping-pong buffer (the Chhugani et al. / Kim et al. 2009, Balkesen 2013 and Inoue 2015 approach the report cites). Key-value pairs use masked compares on the key lanes and blends that move each value with its key; 32-bit int pairs are packed into one int64 and sorted as int64. The merge-pass loop carries an OpenMP parallel for, which is the multicore mode.
when_to_use: Studying or porting a compact AVX-512 bitonic sort-and-merge implementation, including masked key-value networks; the report explains each building block

Sorting power-of-two batches of plain 32-bit ints or floats that already sit in 64-byte-aligned buffers on an AVX-512 x86-64 machine, where the report shows 5.7x (1024 elements) to 7.7x (2^20 elements) over std::sort
Experiments where a data-oblivious, branch-free sort is wanted, since the network does the same work whatever the input order
As a baseline to compare a newer SIMD sort against, not as a production dependency
when_not_to_use: Arbitrary sizes: N must be a power of two and the code only asserts N % 256 == 0, so other sizes read and write past the end (issue #1, open since 2018, reports reads past a 2,000,000-float array)

Large arrays: in the report's own 2^24-element ('10M') AVX-512 table it is only 1.9x std::sort on 32-bit ints, slower than std::sort on 64-bit ints, 32-bit and 64-bit int key-value pairs and 64-bit float pairs, and sequential ips4o beats it on 7 of 8 settings (32-bit ints 0.0755 s vs 0.284 s)
64-bit key-value pairs: slower than std::sort at 2^20 (0.107 s vs 0.085 s for int64 pairs) and far behind ips4o

Production code: unmaintained since May 2018 (later commits only added a licence), leaks a full-size buffer on every call, needs -march=native at build time with no runtime CPU dispatch, and has no NaN handling documented for float keys
Records or custom comparators: only built-in numeric keys, ascending order, one key column

integration.dependencies: OpenMP (omp.h is included by common.h; code is built with -fopenmp); GoogleTest, ips4o and pdqsort only for the bundled tests
integration.min_toolchain: C++14 (CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD 14), CMake 3.5, a GCC- or Clang-style compiler providing x86intrin.h and -march=native; tested compiler and version not documented
integration.platforms: x86-64 only: AVX-512F for avx512::SIMDSort, AVX2 for avx2::SIMDSort, selected at compile time by __AVX512F__/__AVX2__
integration.thread_safety: not documented; no global mutable state, but every merge pass opens an OpenMP parallel region, so the README tells users to set OMP_NUM_THREADS=1 for single-core use

gotchas: Pointer-swapping API: MergeRuns swaps the caller's pointer with an internal posix_memalign buffer after each pass, so when the pass count is odd (int64 or double at 2^20: 17 passes; at the default test size 65536: 13) the caller's pointer comes back pointing at a new buffer, the original memory holds the second-to-last pass and is no longer referenced; the other buffer is never freed, so every call leaks N elements (key-value paths leak two buffers of 2N)

Loads and stores dereference __m512i pointers directly, which compiles to aligned moves: input must be 64-byte aligned (the tests use posix_memalign through aligned_init) or the program faults; the harness then releases these buffers with delete, which is undefined behaviour

Min/max, load/store and network helpers are ordinary functions in separate .cpp files, so the measured speed depends on -flto inlining them across translation units, as in the report's -O3 -flto build

Benchmark harness: single-shot currentSeconds() timings with inputs seeded from std::random_device; integer inputs are drawn from only 20,001 values ([-10000, 10000]), which flatters duplicate-aware comparison sorts at 2^24 (std::sort 0.545 s on ints vs 1.76 s on floats) and makes the 1M-int win the best case; the report's '10M' rows are actually 2^24 = 16.8M elements
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick Highway vqsort or numpy/x86-simd-sort for real AVX-512 sorting: they take any length, dispatch at run time and are maintained; pick IPS4o for large or duplicate-heavy inputs, which beat Ultra-Sort at 2^24 in Ultra-Sort's own report. Ultra-Sort is only the better choice as a small, readable reference for bitonic merge networks and masked key-value sorting.
verified_claims_summary: In the authors' gtest harness on a Xeon Silver 4114 (Skylake-SP), built with -O3 -flto -march=native by an unnamed compiler and standard library, one thread, one timed run each: 2^20 32-bit ints from [-10000, 10000] sorted in 10.4 ms by avx512::sort vs 80.2 ms for std::sort (7.7x), 36.1 ms for pdqsort and 35.4 ms for sequential ips4o. The gain shrinks to 1.9x std::sort at 2^24 elements, where ips4o is 3.8x faster than avx512::sort, and 64-bit key-value sorts lose to std::sort at both sizes.
status_note: Abandoned: last code commit May 2018 (licence added January 2019), issue #1 about out-of-bounds reads for non-power-of-two sizes still open; MIT-licensed and small enough to vendor for study, but the pointer-swapping, leaking API and missing size checks rule it out for production use without rework.
